EPIDEMICS AT THE BORDER: HEALTH SURVEILLANCE, SECURITY AUTHORITY AND TRANSNATIONAL COOPERATION IN EAST AFRICA
Author attribution and institutional affiliation: to be confirmed.
DOI: to be assigned upon publication.
Abstract
Background: Epidemic surveillance along East African borders links infectious-disease detection to authority over movement, markets and citizenship. 
Objective: This article investigates how governments can coordinate outbreak control without making border security an instrument of indiscriminate exclusion. 
Methods: A comparative, documentary mixed-methods synthesis examines published World Health Organization and Uganda government outbreak data, with attention to Sudan virus disease in Uganda, mpox in the African Region, and cholera in South Sudan and neighbouring countries. Descriptive rates and changes are recalculated only where case definitions and reporting cut-offs permit. 
Results: Uganda’s 2025 Sudan virus disease outbreak comprised 14 cases (12 confirmed and two probable), four deaths, and 534 monitored contacts. The WHO African Region reported 10,953 confirmed mpox cases in 2024 by 3 November and 14,849 by 1 December, demonstrating rapidly evolving surveillance totals rather than a controlled trend. South Sudan reported 14,190 cholera cases and 122 deaths between January and August 2026. 
Conclusions: Timely surveillance and information exchange require trusted, interoperable institutions; published aggregate figures cannot isolate the causal effect of border closures or specific policing practices. This paper develops a testable governance model combining timeliness, proportionality, reciprocity and accountability.
Keywords: border health; epidemic surveillance; South Sudan; Uganda; mpox; cholera; Sudan virus disease; regional security; public authority; transnational cooperation.
1. Introduction
Cross-border outbreaks are not simply biological events moving across lines on a map. They are social and administrative crises that expose disagreements over who may move, who must report symptoms, which authority controls a crossing, and which agency pays for testing and care. A person seeking treatment, a trader crossing for a market day and a displaced household escaping conflict encounter the border in sharply different ways. Surveillance that ignores these differences can increase concealment, delay presentation and reduce the credibility of public-health messaging.
East Africa offers an unusually instructive setting. Population mobility crosses formal points of entry and informal pathways, while policing, customs, local councils, humanitarian actors and health services work through overlapping mandates. In stable periods those overlaps may facilitate practical negotiation; during epidemics they can create legal uncertainty and inconsistent restrictions. The analytical problem is therefore not whether a state possesses the formal power to impose health measures, but when coercive power adds public-health value and when it creates avoidable vulnerability.
The empirical cases considered here should not be collapsed into one homogeneous epidemic. Uganda’s 2025 Sudan virus disease outbreak was comparatively small in case count but required intensive contact tracing. Mpox reporting in the WHO African Region covered multiple states and was conditioned by laboratory capacity and evolving case definitions. Cholera in South Sudan involved sustained disease burden against a backdrop of displacement and water, sanitation and hygiene constraints. The variation allows the article to examine institutional mechanisms without pretending that disease-specific rates are directly comparable.
This article has four aims: to identify the documented magnitude and reporting characteristics of selected outbreaks; to explain how border measures redistribute authority and risk; to derive operational indicators for effective cross-border cooperation; and to propose a credible empirical design for future testing. Its contribution is a governance argument rather than a claim that the documentary evidence reveals causal effects. It joins quantitative description to a narrative explanation of why cooperation depends on more than border guards and laboratory equipment.
2. Theoretical and institutional framework
2.1 Securitisation and proportionality
The securitisation perspective explains why exceptional threats justify extraordinary rules, but it also warns that emergency classification can expand discretion without clear limits. Border screening may be warranted when it detects infectious cases and connects patients to care. It becomes counterproductive when it treats mobility itself as culpability. A proportionality test therefore asks whether the health benefit is evidence-based, whether a less restrictive alternative exists, whether the restriction is reviewed, and whether appeal or redress remains accessible.
For comparative research, this mechanism should be measured alongside resources and outbreak severity rather than assumed from policy documents alone. Official directives reveal rules on paper, whereas interviews, facility logs and crossing observations are needed to establish how the rules were experienced by travellers and local providers.
2.2 Polycentric public authority
Surveillance depends on actors operating at multiple levels: national ministries, district health teams, laboratories, immigration agencies, humanitarian organisations, community networks and international institutions. These actors do not merely implement one vertical command. They negotiate jurisdiction, share scarce transport and communication resources, and sometimes compete over data ownership. Polycentric coordination works best when responsibilities and minimum information standards are mutually recognised.
For comparative research, this mechanism should be measured alongside resources and outbreak severity rather than assumed from policy documents alone. Official directives reveal rules on paper, whereas interviews, facility logs and crossing observations are needed to establish how the rules were experienced by travellers and local providers.
2.3 Trust, reporting and the detection paradox
Improved surveillance can initially increase reported cases, not because transmission rises but because previously unseen infections become visible. This detection paradox complicates performance assessment: fewer reported cases do not necessarily mean stronger border controls. The appropriate measures include testing accessibility, reporting delay, investigation coverage and linkage to treatment, as well as incidence. A rise in notifications following improved outreach may be consistent with better public protection.
For comparative research, this mechanism should be measured alongside resources and outbreak severity rather than assumed from policy documents alone. Official directives reveal rules on paper, whereas interviews, facility logs and crossing observations are needed to establish how the rules were experienced by travellers and local providers.
2.4 Regional reciprocity
A useful cross-border compact has reciprocal obligations. Authorities on one side notify their counterparts promptly, while the receiving jurisdiction guarantees that notification will not automatically result in punishment of patients or withholding of essential services. Reciprocal arrangements also require data safeguards: nominal records should be shared only when necessary for a lawful public-health purpose, with clear retention and access rules.
For comparative research, this mechanism should be measured alongside resources and outbreak severity rather than assumed from policy documents alone. Official directives reveal rules on paper, whereas interviews, facility logs and crossing observations are needed to establish how the rules were experienced by travellers and local providers.
2.5 Normative anchors
The International Health Regulations (2005), as amended, frame obligations around detecting, assessing, notifying and responding to risks while seeking to avoid unnecessary interference with international traffic and trade. They do not mandate blanket closures as an automatic response to every outbreak. Operational decisions should reflect the pathogen, transmission route and prevailing evidence; policy instruments that are useful for one disease may be unjustified for another.
For comparative research, this mechanism should be measured alongside resources and outbreak severity rather than assumed from policy documents alone. Official directives reveal rules on paper, whereas interviews, facility logs and crossing observations are needed to establish how the rules were experienced by travellers and local providers.
3. Data and methods
The study uses a structured documentary comparison rather than newly collected field observations. Core primary sources are WHO disease-outbreak notices, WHO Africa mpox bulletins and weekly cholera reports, together with Uganda Ministry of Health statements. Evidence was selected for transparent dates, numerical definitions and relevance to cross-border governance. Sources are reported with their original cut-off dates; later cumulative totals are not substituted silently for earlier values.
The statistical component is descriptive. We calculate reported case fatality as deaths divided by reported cases multiplied by 100, and temporal increases as (later cumulative count − earlier count) divided by earlier count multiplied by 100. These calculations concern reported surveillance data, not population infection fatality rates. Differences between geographical coverage, laboratory confirmation and probable case inclusion preclude pooling disease-specific case-fatality ratios into a single regional estimate.
Analysis proceeds through four domains: detection and notification, cross-border coordination, exercise of security powers, and protection of affected populations. Narrative evidence is used to identify plausible causal pathways and rival interpretations. Because we have no individual-level interviews, journey-level crossing records or harmonised policy-timing database, the study cannot infer that a border policy directly caused a particular mortality or case-count change.
An empirical follow-on design is offered to make the framework falsifiable. Its suggested unit of observation is the border crossing-week, nested within district and country. Prospective variables include time from notification to investigation, laboratory turnaround, proportion of referrals completed, hours of crossing restriction, essential-travel exemption rates, complaint volume and traveller-reported trust. Pre-registration should define outcomes and confounders before data are analysed.
4. Quantitative findings and interpretation
Table 1. Uganda 2025 Sudan virus disease outbreak
Indicator | Value | Reporting rule
Confirmed cases | 12 | Laboratory confirmed
Probable cases | 2 | Not laboratory confirmed
Total cases | 14 | Confirmed + probable
Deaths | 4 | 2 confirmed + 2 probable
Monitored contacts | 534 | Identified and followed
Recovered patients | 10 | Reported recovered
Source and notes: WHO (26 April 2025); Uganda Ministry of Health (26 April 2025).
Interpretation. The proportion of total reported cases who died was 4/14 = 28.6%; the confirmed-only share was 2/12 = 16.7%. Neither is an infection-fatality estimate. Intensive monitoring of 534 contacts for 14 cases illustrates the labour demands of containment, but contacts per case is not a measure of transmission because contact sets overlap and tracing coverage depends on ascertainment.
Figure 1. 2025 Uganda SVD case outcomes
Figure interpretation. Reported categories overlap: deaths are within total cases, not additional cases. The chart should therefore be read as separate surveillance indicators, not as a partition of the full case population.
Uganda declared the outbreak over after 42 days without a new confirmed case following the final negative test/discharge milestone. This is best understood as an outbreak-specific stopping rule supported by surveillance, not a universal calendar duration for every pathogen. The government and WHO simultaneously emphasised continued monitoring after the official declaration, indicating that cessation of emergency classification need not mean disappearance of institutional vigilance.
Table 2. WHO Africa 2024 mpox reporting at distinct publication cut-offs
WHO cut-off | Confirmed 2024 cases | Confirmed deaths | Coverage
3 November 2024 | 10953 | 53 | 18 countries
17 November 2024 | 13293 | 54 | 19 countries
1 December 2024 | 14849 | 58 | 19 countries
Source and notes: WHO Regional Mpox Bulletins dated 3 November, 18 November (data to 17 Nov), and 1 December 2024.
Interpretation. Between the first and last bulletin the reported cumulative count rose by 3,896 cases, or 35.6% relative to the earlier count. The changing country coverage and surveillance practices mean this is a growth in reported confirmed totals, not a precisely estimated growth rate in underlying infections. Diagnostic availability may change independently of true transmission.
Figure 2. Mpox confirmed cases at successive WHO 2024 cut-offs
Figure interpretation. The line connects publication cut-offs, not equal-duration epidemiological measurement intervals. It illustrates the accumulation and revision of surveillance totals, which should be paired with testing coverage and case definitions before causal claims are made.
Table 3. Selected WHO cholera reports, January–May 2026
Country | Reported cases | Deaths | Reported CFR (%)
South Sudan | 7712 | 84 | 1.09
DR Congo | 28567 | 815 | 2.85
Burundi | 1163 | 2 | 0.17
Kenya | 26 | 0 | 0
Tanzania | 113 | 2 | 1.77
Source and notes: WHO Weekly Epidemiological Record 101-26, data through 31 May 2026. Ratios calculated from published counts.
Interpretation. These are distinct national disease burdens, not confirmed cross-border transmission chains. The substantial differences reflect population size, epidemic geography, case detection and care conditions. Kenya’s 26 cases with no reported deaths are insufficient to infer zero clinical risk, while DR Congo’s high absolute death count points to the need for context-specific analysis of access to treatment.
Figure 3. 2026 cholera cases in selected countries (May cumulative)
Figure interpretation. Absolute cases illustrate reported burden but cannot rank risk to an individual traveller without population denominators, testing intensity and comparable observation windows.
Table 4. South Sudan 2026 cholera accumulation
Cut-off | Cases Jan–cut-off | Deaths | Case-fatality ratio
28 June 2026 | 10526 | 111 | 1.05%
30 August 2026 | 14190 | 122 | 0.86%
Source and notes: WHO WER 101-31 and WER 101-39. Both are cumulative from 1 January 2026.
Interpretation. The increase between the two cut-offs is 3,664 cases and 11 additional reported deaths. The cumulative CFR fell arithmetically from 1.05% to 0.86%, but this does not demonstrate improved clinical effectiveness, because ascertainment, reporting delays and composition of cases can change. In August WHO reported concentration of transmission in Unity and Upper Nile, with displacement and WASH constraints relevant to the spatial pattern.
Figure 4. South Sudan 2026 cholera cumulative cases (June–August)
Figure interpretation. The cumulative case burden increased by 34.8% between the two cut-offs. This statistic is a comparison of cumulative reports over roughly two months and should not be confused with an average monthly incidence rate.
Table 5. Operational indicators for cooperative border surveillance
Domain | Measurable indicator | Interpretive limitation
Timeliness | Median hours from alert to cross-border notice | Depends on first-alert recording
Completeness | Share of contact referrals closed with feedback | Affected by address quality
Proportionality | Restriction hours per verified risk episode | Requires pathogen-specific criteria
Equity | Share of suspected cases receiving care regardless of status | Facility access varies
Trust | Anonymous traveller confidence scale | Selection and fear bias
Source and notes: Authors’ proposed monitoring framework; indicators are not measured empirical results.
Interpretation. This table is not evidence of achieved regional performance. It operationalises the political argument by identifying how security power, reciprocal communication and rights-based care could be assessed in a future multicountry design. Measures should be disaggregated by gender, mobility status and crossing type where privacy protection permits.
Figure 5. Uganda 2025 contact tracing and outcomes
Figure interpretation. The large count of monitored contacts relative to cases reflects workload and surveillance scope. It must not be read as 534 infections, nor should a tracing ratio be treated as a substitute for a contact follow-up completion rate.
Figure 6. Comparative reported cholera fatality ratios, August 2026
Figure interpretation. The August 2026 WHO comparisons use January–August totals and show markedly different reported case fatality ratios; they do not establish why the differences occurred. Variations in ascertainment, case management, displacement and reporting completeness are important alternative explanations.
5. Narrative synthesis: where disease control meets political power
5.1 The border as a surveillance network rather than a wall
A purely territorial conception of epidemic response prioritises keeping pathogens outside a jurisdiction. Yet exposure, incubation and informal mobility patterns mean biological risk is not exhausted by the formal port of entry. A network conception instead emphasises interoperable notification, continuity of care and transport of specimens. Health posts can become useful nodes of detection when individuals believe that disclosing symptoms will lead to assistance rather than indiscriminate detention or punitive treatment.
A field-based test should therefore compare formal policy with everyday implementation. Researchers would need timestamped notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed, which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.
5.2 The paradox of exceptional enforcement
Emergency powers can accelerate inspection and data exchange, but blunt enforcement may displace travel to less visible crossings. A reduction in recorded movement through an official gate might represent successful compliance, displacement of routes or declining economic activity; the administrative count alone cannot distinguish the interpretations. Evaluations need mobility proxies, interviews and information about changes in lawful crossing access.
A field-based test should therefore compare formal policy with everyday implementation. Researchers would need timestamped notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed, which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.
5.3 Trade, food security and proportionality
A border restriction may interrupt essential trade and complicate healthcare for patients who routinely use facilities across an international frontier. A defensible decision framework weighs expected transmission prevention against interruption to medicines, food distribution and income. The relevant counterfactual is not unrestricted movement without surveillance, but less restrictive interventions such as targeted screening, referral pathways, risk communication and structured exemptions.
A field-based test should therefore compare formal policy with everyday implementation. Researchers would need timestamped notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed, which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.
5.4 Displacement and unequal exposure
South Sudan’s cholera burden underscores the importance of crowding, service access and water systems. Displaced people often face greater difficulty obtaining documentation, transport and reliable communications, which may limit timely care. A security-first response may intensify those barriers unless health authorities coordinate with humanitarian services and community-based organisations. Not all displacement-associated transmission is attributable to crossing an international border.
A field-based test should therefore compare formal policy with everyday implementation. Researchers would need timestamped notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed, which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.
5.5 The politics of numbers
Published counts are administrative products. Confirmed cases depend on access to testing, probable cases depend on case definition, deaths depend on recording practices, and contacts depend on interview quality. Consequently, the best governance signal may be a set of linked indicators rather than a single case total. Comparing raw totals between outbreaks with different diagnostics can falsely reward under-detection.
A field-based test should therefore compare formal policy with everyday implementation. Researchers would need timestamped notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed, which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.
5.6 Trust and shared authority
Legitimate public-health authority is exercised through predictable rules and reason-giving. Border communities may comply more readily when they participate in risk communication and when multilingual instructions are consistent across ministries. Bilateral coordination should include frontline clinicians, transport workers and civil society, not simply senior security agencies. Where communities have experienced arbitrary restrictions, credible complaints mechanisms become part of outbreak preparedness.
A field-based test should therefore compare formal policy with everyday implementation. Researchers would need timestamped notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed, which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. 5.7 Data exchange without surveillance overreach
Sharing personal identifiers can be necessary for contact tracing, but indefinite retention or generalised law-enforcement access can undermine willingness to report. Agreements should specify disease-control purposes, minimum necessary data, secure transfer, deletion schedules and independent oversight. Regional interoperability should mean that health personnel can safely act on alerts, not that all traveller information becomes permanently available to unrelated agencies.
A field-based test should therefore compare formal policy with everyday implementation. Researchers would need timestamped notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed, which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. 5.8 Avoiding the false choice between sovereignty and cooperation
National authorities retain responsibility for their populations, yet pathogen circulation makes unilateral success contingent on neighbouring systems. Reciprocity can preserve sovereignty by making obligations explicit and accountable. The shared benefit is a shorter time between detection, notification and clinical action. This is a narrower and more measurable aim than claiming that regional cooperation always eliminates outbreaks.

Researchers would need timestamped notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed, which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. 6. Proposed quantitative and qualitative research extension
6.1 Units and sampling
Select matched crossing points in Uganda–South Sudan, Kenya–Uganda and other relevant corridors, balancing high-volume official gates with accessible community pathways. Observe crossing-week records over comparable surveillance periods and stratify by pathogen and outbreak phase. A priori power calculations depend on observed baseline notification delays and within-crossing clustering; arbitrary sample sizes would be inappropriate.
The resulting dataset should preserve a public codebook, versioned source references and an auditable distinction between missing observations and recorded zeros. Where national totals have been retrospectively revised, the analysis should retain the original vintage alongside the corrected release. This would permit external readers to understand exactly which figures underlie each visualisation and estimate.
6.2 Measurement and model
Primary outcome Y_it could be log(1 + hours from first alert to completed referral) at crossing i and week t. A preregistered specification is Y_it = α_i + δ_t + β1 JointProtocol_it + β2 Staffing_it + β3 TestAvailability_it + β4 Mobility_it + ε_it. Crossing and calendar fixed effects could adjust for stable site characteristics and shared shocks. Joint protocols are likely adopted in response to risk, so β1 would not automatically be causal; a defensible identification strategy must document policy timing and parallel trends.
The resulting dataset should preserve a public codebook, versioned source references and an auditable distinction between missing observations and recorded zeros. Where national totals have been retrospectively revised, the analysis should retain the original vintage alongside the corrected release. This would permit external readers to understand exactly which figures underlie each visualisation and estimate.
6.3 Qualitative component
Semi-structured interviews should ask clinicians, border officers, transport associations and travellers how alerts are communicated and how exemptions are applied. Interviews should be voluntary, anonymised and conducted away from authorities who control respondents’ movement. Negative cases—sites with nominal cooperation but poor referrals, or informal routes with effective community reporting—may be especially informative.
The resulting dataset should preserve a public codebook, versioned source references and an auditable distinction between missing observations and recorded zeros. Where national totals have been retrospectively revised, the analysis should retain the original vintage alongside the corrected release. This would permit external readers to understand exactly which figures underlie each visualisation and estimate.
6.4 Ethics and safeguarding
Research must not collect identifiable infection histories or movement routes without compelling scientific necessity and formal approval. Consent should distinguish medical service access from research participation, ensuring refusal does not affect care or legal status. Small-cell suppression is essential where disaggregated disease or migration data could identify individuals. Security actors should not receive raw interview recordings.
The resulting dataset should preserve a public codebook, versioned source references and an auditable distinction between missing observations and recorded zeros. Where national totals have been retrospectively revised, the analysis should retain the original vintage alongside the corrected release. This would permit external readers to understand exactly which figures underlie each visualisation and estimate.
6.5 Robustness and competing explanations
Sensitivity analyses could examine alternative outcome windows, excluding weeks with laboratory shutdowns, and different definitions of notified alerts. Disease-specific analyses are preferable to pooled regressions unless interaction terms and substantive differences are justified. Interrupted time-series designs should account for concurrent vaccination, changes in testing supply, seasonal mobility and conflict interruptions.
The resulting dataset should preserve a public codebook, versioned source references and an auditable distinction between missing observations and recorded zeros. Where national totals have been retrospectively revised, the analysis should retain the original vintage alongside the corrected release. This would permit external readers to understand exactly which figures underlie each visualisation and estimate.
6.6 Field instrument: minimum variables
A crossing-week sheet should record gate identifier (pseudonymised), week, pathogen, total alerts, test availability days, sample turnaround distribution, notifications forwarded, notifications acknowledged, completed clinical referrals, restriction hours, cross-border meetings and written complaints. No identifiable person-level health data are necessary to calculate many of these indicators.
The resulting dataset should preserve a public codebook, versioned source references and an auditable distinction between missing observations and recorded zeros. Where national totals have been retrospectively revised, the analysis should retain the original vintage alongside the corrected release. This would permit external readers to understand exactly which figures underlie each visualisation and estimate.
6.7 Interview and document review guide
Interview prompts should elicit a chronological description of the most recent alert; the last communication bottleneck; authority for imposing restrictions; eligibility for essential-travel exceptions; arrangements for undocumented travellers; methods of correcting misinformation; and the procedure for handling data-security breaches. Documentary review should compare signed protocols with actual logs and after-action reports.
The resulting dataset should preserve a public codebook, versioned source references and an auditable distinction between missing observations and recorded zeros. Where national totals have been retrospectively revised, the analysis should retain the original vintage alongside the corrected release. This would permit external readers to understand exactly which figures underlie each visualisation and estimate.
7. Discussion
The findings challenge three convenient assumptions. First, the effectiveness of surveillance cannot be reduced to counting people screened. The Uganda Sudan virus disease episode demonstrates that contact tracing may involve hundreds of individuals even when the reported number of cases remains low. Second, stronger detection may increase reported case counts in the short term, making simplistic rankings of administrations misleading. Third, public-health authority is not synonymous with unrestricted security discretion; timely care and credible communication are operational dimensions of state capacity.
The comparison also illustrates the danger of treating all transboundary pathogens as equivalent. Sudan virus disease requires case identification and contact management under a specific incubation and transmission profile. Mpox surveillance depends on testing, case definitions and community engagement. Cholera is inseparable from safe water, sanitation and treatment access. A border regime built for only one threat may inadequately address the others or impose disproportionate costs.
An original conceptual contribution is the reciprocal surveillance compact: a set of measurable commitments joining alert timeliness to clinical referral, mobility safeguards, data minimisation and accountable oversight. Unlike an abstract plea for regional unity, the compact specifies observable obligations. Its performance remains a hypothesis requiring longitudinal implementation evidence, not a statistical effect demonstrated by the country-level figures in this manuscript.
For East African institutions, meaningful cooperation should involve harmonised alert vocabulary, training at paired crossings, shared simulation exercises and community-level monitoring of the effects of restrictive measures. Such initiatives should be assessed not by meeting counts alone but by changes in notification delays, referral completion and patient safety, with attention to unequal consequences for displaced and undocumented populations.
8. Limitations
The study synthesises aggregate, published information rather than original respondent or facility data. WHO publications use differing reporting windows and disease-specific case definitions, and some counts are retrospectively revised. Certain cross-country comparisons are illustrative of reporting structures rather than like-for-like measures of infection risk. No causal association between a particular border intervention and epidemic outcomes is claimed. Proposed regression models, indicators and field instruments require ethical approval, feasibility testing and access to independently verifiable observations.
9. Conclusion and policy implications
Cross-border health surveillance in East Africa is a problem of institutional trust and legitimate authority as well as epidemiology. Uganda’s 2025 Sudan virus disease outbreak and regional mpox and cholera data illuminate the demands placed on case detection, reporting systems and health services; they do not provide a licence to infer that more coercive border control is necessarily more effective. A credible model combines rapid communication, proportionate restrictions, continuity of care and protection of individual information. Future research should test whether reciprocal agreements improve referral timeliness and equitable service access under real outbreak conditions.
10. Implementation roadmap and evaluation criteria
10.1 First 90 days: map authority and referral routes
A feasible preparatory phase would identify paired facilities, district surveillance focal persons, laboratory transport pathways, customs and immigration decision-makers, and civil-society liaison contacts at each crossing. For every existing memorandum, the coordinating team should record the official signatories, current operational contacts, emergency number, minimum alert content and acknowledgement rule. This baseline exercise should avoid inventing an entirely new command hierarchy where one already functions. Instead, it should reveal duplicated approvals and gaps between written arrangements and actual practice. Simulation exercises should include ordinary travellers, undocumented patients and time-sensitive medical referrals so that the rights implications of emergency powers become visible before an outbreak.
Measurement quality is part of implementation: an independent audit should compare a sample of dashboard entries against contemporaneous registers, document discrepancies and revise procedures without replacing the original figures invisibly. This protects the integrity of both programme management and future peer-reviewed research.
10.2 Months four to six: rehearse the alert-to-care chain
Paired border health teams could conduct structured tabletop exercises using non-identifiable scenarios for a suspected case, a laboratory-confirmed result and an exposure discovered after travel. The exercise should timestamp alert receipt, risk assessment, counterpart notification, clinical referral and feedback. Debriefs should distinguish avoidable administrative waiting time from time required for testing or clinical stabilisation. A shared after-action report should record actions agreed and persons responsible, but need not contain real patient information. Where power or mobile-network outages affect communication, an agreed backup channel should be tested and documented.
Measurement quality is part of implementation: an independent audit should compare a sample of dashboard entries against contemporaneous registers, document discrepancies and revise procedures without replacing the original figures invisibly. This protects the integrity of both programme management and future peer-reviewed research.
10.3 Months seven to twelve: monitor performance fairly
A dashboard should display monthly distributions rather than only averages: median referral completion hours, interquartile ranges, proportion of notifications acknowledged within a preregistered threshold, and complaint closure time. Results should be stratified by crossing site and outbreak phase, with explanatory annotations for laboratory closures or exceptionally heavy movement. Aggregate public reporting can strengthen accountability while limiting identification risk. A falling count of suspected cases should never stand alone as evidence of progress; reduced access to screening can create the same pattern. External review should examine both epidemiological indicators and the experience of people crossing for care or livelihood.
Measurement quality is part of implementation: an independent audit should compare a sample of dashboard entries against contemporaneous registers, document discrepancies and revise procedures without replacing the original figures invisibly. This protects the integrity of both programme management and future peer-reviewed research.
10.4 Governance safeguards and escalation
The cross-border compact should distinguish clinical decisions from border-enforcement decisions. Health practitioners must be able to recommend care without automatic punitive referral. Restrictions need a written legal basis, review date, reason-giving and an accessible route for complaints. Data-sharing officers should maintain access logs and conduct periodic deletion reviews. An escalation protocol must specify which agency resolves disagreement when neighbouring authorities classify the same event differently, and how urgent patient referral continues during that disagreement. These controls do not weaken disease protection; they make cooperation more predictable and therefore easier to sustain.
Measurement quality is part of implementation: an independent audit should compare a sample of dashboard entries against contemporaneous registers, document discrepancies and revise procedures without replacing the original figures invisibly. This protects the integrity of both programme management and future peer-reviewed research.
10.5 What would count as a policy success
The proposed indicators should register joint improvements in three dimensions: verified shortening of alert-to-referral time, maintenance of access to essential care across mobility-status categories, and reduction in unjustified restrictive practices. No single composite index should hide deterioration in equity behind gains in administrative speed. Policymakers should require a minimum acceptable score in each domain before declaring a pilot successful. External researchers can then use phased implementation and comparable sites to assess whether the improvements persist after initial training support is withdrawn.

This protects the integrity of both programme management and future peer-reviewed research.

Abstract
Background: Epidemic surveillance along East African borders links infectious-disease detection to authority over movement, markets
and citizenship.
Objective: This article investigates how governments can coordinate outbreak control without making border security an instrument of
indiscriminate exclusion.
Methods: A comparative, documentary mixed-methods synthesis examines published World Health Organization and Uganda
government outbreak data, with attention to Sudan virus disease in Uganda, mpox in the African Region, and cholera in South Sudan
and neighbouring countries. Descriptive rates and changes are recalculated only where case definitions and reporting cut-offs permit.
Results: Uganda’s 2025 Sudan virus disease outbreak comprised 14 cases (12 confirmed and two probable), four deaths, and 534
monitored contacts. The WHO African Region reported 10,953 confirmed mpox cases in 2024 by 3 November and 14,849 by 1 December,
demonstrating rapidly evolving surveillance totals rather than a controlled trend. South Sudan reported 14,190 cholera cases and 122
deaths between January and August 2026.
Conclusions: Timely surveillance and information exchange require trusted, interoperable institutions; published aggregate figures
cannot isolate the causal effect of border closures or specific policing practices. This paper develops a testable governance model
combining timeliness, proportionality, reciprocity and accountability.
Keywords: border health; epidemic surveillance; South Sudan; Uganda; mpox; cholera; Sudan virus disease; regional security; public
authority; transnational cooperation.

1. Introduction
Cross-border outbreaks are not simply biological events moving across lines on a map. They are social and administrative crises that
expose disagreements over who may move, who must report symptoms, which authority controls a crossing, and which agency pays for
testing and care. A person seeking treatment, a trader crossing for a market day and a displaced household escaping conflict encounter
the border in sharply different ways. Surveillance that ignores these differences can increase concealment, delay presentation and
reduce the credibility of public-health messaging.
East Africa offers an unusually instructive setting. Population mobility crosses formal points of entry and informal pathways, while
policing, customs, local councils, humanitarian actors and health services work through overlapping mandates. In stable periods those
overlaps may facilitate practical negotiation; during epidemics they can create legal uncertainty and inconsistent restrictions. The
analytical problem is therefore not whether a state possesses the formal power to impose health measures, but when coercive power
adds public-health value and when it creates avoidable vulnerability.

 The empirical cases considered here should not be collapsed into one homogeneous epidemic. Uganda’s 2025 Sudan virus disease
outbreak was comparatively small in case count but required intensive contact tracing. Mpox reporting in the WHO African Region
covered multiple states and was conditioned by laboratory capacity and evolving case definitions. Cholera in South Sudan involved
sustained disease burden against a backdrop of displacement and water, sanitation and hygiene constraints. The variation allows the
article to examine institutional mechanisms without pretending that disease-specific rates are directly comparable.
This article has four aims: to identify the documented magnitude and reporting characteristics of selected outbreaks; to explain how
border measures redistribute authority and risk; to derive operational indicators for effective cross-border cooperation; and to propose
a credible empirical design for future testing. Its contribution is a governance argument rather than a claim that the documentary
evidence reveals causal effects. It joins quantitative description to a narrative explanation of why cooperation depends on more than
border guards and laboratory equipment.

2. Theoretical and institutional framework
2.1 Securitisation and proportionality
The securitisation perspective explains why exceptional threats justify extraordinary rules, but it also warns that emergency
classification can expand discretion without clear limits. Border screening may be warranted when it detects infectious cases and
connects patients to care. It becomes counterproductive when it treats mobility itself as culpability. A proportionality test therefore asks
whether the health benefit is evidence-based, whether a less restrictive alternative exists, whether the restriction is reviewed, and
whether appeal or redress remains accessible.
For comparative research, this mechanism should be measured alongside resources and outbreak severity rather than assumed from
policy documents alone. Official directives reveal rules on paper, whereas interviews, facility logs and crossing observations are needed
to establish how the rules were experienced by travellers and local providers.

2.2 Polycentric public authority
Surveillance depends on actors operating at multiple levels: national ministries, district health teams, laboratories, immigration
agencies, humanitarian organisations, community networks and international institutions. These actors do not merely implement one
vertical command. They negotiate jurisdiction, share scarce transport and communication resources, and sometimes compete over data
ownership. Polycentric coordination works best when responsibilities and minimum information standards are mutually recognised.
For comparative research, this mechanism should be measured alongside resources and outbreak severity rather than assumed from
policy documents alone. Official directives reveal rules on paper, whereas interviews, facility logs and crossing observations are needed
to establish how the rules were experienced by travellers and local providers.

2.3 Trust, reporting and the detection paradox
Improved surveillance can initially increase reported cases, not because transmission rises but because previously unseen infections
become visible. This detection paradox complicates performance assessment: fewer reported cases do not necessarily mean stronger
border controls. The appropriate measures include testing accessibility, reporting delay, investigation coverage and linkage to
treatment, as well as incidence. A rise in notifications following improved outreach may be consistent with better public protection.
For comparative research, this mechanism should be measured alongside resources and outbreak severity rather than assumed from
policy documents alone. Official directives reveal rules on paper, whereas interviews, facility logs and crossing observations are needed
to establish how the rules were experienced by travellers and local providers.

2.4 Regional reciprocity
A useful cross-border compact has reciprocal obligations. Authorities on one side notify their counterparts promptly, while the
receiving jurisdiction guarantees that notification will not automatically result in punishment of patients or withholding of essential
services. Reciprocal arrangements also require data safeguards: nominal records should be shared only when necessary for a lawful
public-health purpose, with clear retention and access rules.
For comparative research, this mechanism should be measured alongside resources and outbreak severity rather than assumed from
policy documents alone. Official directives reveal rules on paper, whereas interviews, facility logs and crossing observations are needed
to establish how the rules were experienced by travellers and local providers.

 2.5 Normative anchors
The International Health Regulations (2005), as amended, frame obligations around detecting, assessing, notifying and responding to
risks while seeking to avoid unnecessary interference with international traffic and trade. They do not mandate blanket closures as an
automatic response to every outbreak. Operational decisions should reflect the pathogen, transmission route and prevailing evidence;
policy instruments that are useful for one disease may be unjustified for another.
For comparative research, this mechanism should be measured alongside resources and outbreak severity rather than assumed from
policy documents alone. Official directives reveal rules on paper, whereas interviews, facility logs and crossing observations are needed
to establish how the rules were experienced by travellers and local providers.

3. Data and methods
The study uses a structured documentary comparison rather than newly collected field observations. Core primary sources are WHO
disease-outbreak notices, WHO Africa mpox bulletins and weekly cholera reports, together with Uganda Ministry of Health statements.
Evidence was selected for transparent dates, numerical definitions and relevance to cross-border governance. Sources are reported
with their original cut-off dates; later cumulative totals are not substituted silently for earlier values.
The statistical component is descriptive. We calculate reported case fatality as deaths divided by reported cases multiplied by 100, and
temporal increases as (later cumulative count − earlier count) divided by earlier count multiplied by 100. These calculations concern
reported surveillance data, not population infection fatality rates. Differences between geographical coverage, laboratory confirmation
and probable case inclusion preclude pooling disease-specific case-fatality ratios into a single regional estimate.
Analysis proceeds through four domains: detection and notification, cross-border coordination, exercise of security powers, and
protection of affected populations. Narrative evidence is used to identify plausible causal pathways and rival interpretations. Because
we have no individual-level interviews, journey-level crossing records or harmonised policy-timing database, the study cannot infer
that a border policy directly caused a particular mortality or case-count change.
An empirical follow-on design is offered to make the framework falsifiable. Its suggested unit of observation is the border crossingweek, nested within district and country. Prospective variables include time from notification to investigation, laboratory turnaround,
proportion of referrals completed, hours of crossing restriction, essential-travel exemption rates, complaint volume and travellerreported trust. Pre-registration should define outcomes and confounders before data are analysed.

5. Narrative synthesis: where disease control meets political power
5.1 The border as a surveillance network rather than a wall
A purely territorial conception of epidemic response prioritises keeping pathogens outside a jurisdiction. Yet exposure, incubation and
informal mobility patterns mean biological risk is not exhausted by the formal port of entry. A network conception instead emphasises
interoperable notification, continuity of care and transport of specimens. Health posts can become useful nodes of detection when
individuals believe that disclosing symptoms will lead to assistance rather than indiscriminate detention or punitive treatment.
A field-based test should therefore compare formal policy with everyday implementation. Researchers would need timestamped
notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed,
which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of
such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.

5.2 The paradox of exceptional enforcement
Emergency powers can accelerate inspection and data exchange, but blunt enforcement may displace travel to less visible crossings. A
reduction in recorded movement through an official gate might represent successful compliance, displacement of routes or declining
economic activity; the administrative count alone cannot distinguish the interpretations. Evaluations need mobility proxies, interviews
and information about changes in lawful crossing access.
A field-based test should therefore compare formal policy with everyday implementation. Researchers would need timestamped
notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed,
which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of
such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.

5.3 Trade, food security and proportionality
A border restriction may interrupt essential trade and complicate healthcare for patients who routinely use facilities across an
international frontier. A defensible decision framework weighs expected transmission prevention against interruption to medicines,
food distribution and income. The relevant counterfactual is not unrestricted movement without surveillance, but less restrictive
interventions such as targeted screening, referral pathways, risk communication and structured exemptions.

notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed,
which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of
such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.

5.4 Displacement and unequal exposure
South Sudan’s cholera burden underscores the importance of crowding, service access and water systems. Displaced people often face
greater difficulty obtaining documentation, transport and reliable communications, which may limit timely care. A security-first
response may intensify those barriers unless health authorities coordinate with humanitarian services and community-based
organisations. Not all displacement-associated transmission is attributable to crossing an international border.

notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed,
which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of
such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.

5.5 The politics of numbers
Published counts are administrative products. Confirmed cases depend on access to testing, probable cases depend on case definition,
deaths depend on recording practices, and contacts depend on interview quality. Consequently, the best governance signal may be a set
of linked indicators rather than a single case total. Comparing raw totals between outbreaks with different diagnostics can falsely
reward under-detection.
A field-based test should therefore compare formal policy with everyday implementation. Researchers would need timestamped
notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed,
which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of
such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.

5.6 Trust and shared authority
Legitimate public-health authority is exercised through predictable rules and reason-giving. Border communities may comply more
readily when they participate in risk communication and when multilingual instructions are consistent across ministries. Bilateral
coordination should include frontline clinicians, transport workers and civil society, not simply senior security agencies. Where
communities have experienced arbitrary restrictions, credible complaints mechanisms become part of outbreak preparedness.

notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed,
which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of
such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.

5.7 Data exchange without surveillance overreach
Sharing personal identifiers can be necessary for contact tracing, but indefinite retention or generalised law-enforcement access can
undermine willingness to report. Agreements should specify disease-control purposes, minimum necessary data, secure transfer,
deletion schedules and independent oversight. Regional interoperability should mean that health personnel can safely act on alerts, not
that all traveller information becomes permanently available to unrelated agencies.

notifications, clinic referral registers and interviews at both sides of selected crossings. They should ask which actors were informed,
which travellers received exemptions, and whether information could be acted upon without breaching confidentiality. The absence of
such microdata in the present analysis is acknowledged rather than filled with fabricated testimony.

5.8 Avoiding the false choice between sovereignty and cooperation
National authorities retain responsibility for their populations, yet pathogen circulation makes unilateral success contingent on
neighbouring systems. Reciprocity can preserve sovereignty by making obligations explicit and accountable. The shared benefit is a
shorter time between detection, notification and clinical action. This is a narrower and more measurable aim than claiming that
regional cooperation always eliminates outbreaks.

6. Proposed quantitative and qualitative research extension
6.1 Units and sampling
Select matched crossing points in Uganda–South Sudan, Kenya–Uganda and other relevant corridors, balancing high-volume official
gates with accessible community pathways. Observe crossing-week records over comparable surveillance periods and stratify by
pathogen and outbreak phase. A priori power calculations depend on observed baseline notification delays and within-crossing
clustering; arbitrary sample sizes would be inappropriate.
The resulting dataset should preserve a public codebook, versioned source references and an auditable distinction between missing
observations and recorded zeros. Where national totals have been retrospectively revised, the analysis should retain the original
vintage alongside the corrected release. This would permit external readers to understand exactly which figures underlie each
visualisation and estimate.

Primary outcome Y_it could be log(1 + hours from first alert to completed referral) at crossing i and week t. A preregistered specification
is Y_it = α_i + δ_t + β1 JointProtocol_it + β2 Staffing_it + β3 TestAvailability_it + β4 Mobility_it + ε_it. Crossing and calendar fixed effects
could adjust for stable site characteristics and shared shocks. Joint protocols are likely adopted in response to risk, so β1 would not
automatically be causal; a defensible identification strategy must document policy timing and parallel trends.

6.3 Qualitative component
Semi-structured interviews should ask clinicians, border officers, transport associations and travellers how alerts are communicated
and how exemptions are applied. Interviews should be voluntary, anonymised and conducted away from authorities who control
respondents’ movement. Negative cases—sites with nominal cooperation but poor referrals, or informal routes with effective
community reporting—may be especially informative.

Research must not collect identifiable infection histories or movement routes without compelling scientific necessity and formal
approval. Consent should distinguish medical service access from research participation, ensuring refusal does not affect care or legal
status. Small-cell suppression is essential where disaggregated disease or migration data could identify individuals. Security actors
should not receive raw interview recordings.

Sensitivity analyses could examine alternative outcome windows, excluding weeks with laboratory shutdowns, and different definitions

7. Discussion
The findings challenge three convenient assumptions. First, the effectiveness of surveillance cannot be reduced to counting people
screened. The Uganda Sudan virus disease episode demonstrates that contact tracing may involve hundreds of individuals even when
the reported number of cases remains low. Second, stronger detection may increase reported case counts in the short term, making
simplistic rankings of administrations misleading. Third, public-health authority is not synonymous with unrestricted security
discretion; timely care and credible communication are operational dimensions of state capacity.
The comparison also illustrates the danger of treating all transboundary pathogens as equivalent. Sudan virus disease requires case
identification and contact management under a specific incubation and transmission profile. Mpox surveillance depends on testing,
case definitions and community engagement. Cholera is inseparable from safe water, sanitation and treatment access. A border regime
built for only one threat may inadequately address the others or impose disproportionate costs.
An original conceptual contribution is the reciprocal surveillance compact: a set of measurable commitments joining alert timeliness to
clinical referral, mobility safeguards, data minimisation and accountable oversight. Unlike an abstract plea for regional unity, the
compact specifies observable obligations. Its performance remains a hypothesis requiring longitudinal implementation evidence, not a
statistical effect demonstrated by the country-level figures in this manuscript.
For East African institutions, meaningful cooperation should involve harmonised alert vocabulary, training at paired crossings, shared
simulation exercises and community-level monitoring of the effects of restrictive measures. Such initiatives should be assessed not by
meeting counts alone but by changes in notification delays, referral completion and patient safety, with attention to unequal
consequences for displaced and undocumented populations.

8. Limitations
The study synthesises aggregate, published information rather than original respondent or facility data. WHO publications use differing
reporting windows and disease-specific case definitions, and some counts are retrospectively revised. Certain cross-country

 comparisons are illustrative of reporting structures rather than like-for-like measures of infection risk. No causal association between a
particular border intervention and epidemic outcomes is claimed. Proposed regression models, indicators and field instruments require
ethical approval, feasibility testing and access to independently verifiable observations.

9. Conclusion and policy implications
Cross-border health surveillance in East Africa is a problem of institutional trust and legitimate authority as well as epidemiology.
Uganda’s 2025 Sudan virus disease outbreak and regional mpox and cholera data illuminate the demands placed on case detection,
reporting systems and health services; they do not provide a licence to infer that more coercive border control is necessarily more
effective. A credible model combines rapid communication, proportionate restrictions, continuity of care and protection of individual
information. Future research should test whether reciprocal agreements improve referral timeliness and equitable service access under
real outbreak conditions.

10. Implementation roadmap and evaluation criteria
10.1 First 90 days: map authority and referral routes
A feasible preparatory phase would identify paired facilities, district surveillance focal persons, laboratory transport pathways, customs
and immigration decision-makers, and civil-society liaison contacts at each crossing. For every existing memorandum, the coordinating
team should record the official signatories, current operational contacts, emergency number, minimum alert content and
acknowledgement rule. This baseline exercise should avoid inventing an entirely new command hierarchy where one already
functions. Instead, it should reveal duplicated approvals and gaps between written arrangements and actual practice. Simulation
exercises should include ordinary travellers, undocumented patients and time-sensitive medical referrals so that the rights implications
of emergency powers become visible before an outbreak.
Measurement quality is part of implementation: an independent audit should compare a sample of dashboard entries against
contemporaneous registers, document discrepancies and revise procedures without replacing the original figures invisibly. This
protects the integrity of both programme management and future peer-reviewed research.

10.2 Months four to six: rehearse the alert-to-care chain
Paired border health teams could conduct structured tabletop exercises using non-identifiable scenarios for a suspected case, a
laboratory-confirmed result and an exposure discovered after travel. The exercise should timestamp alert receipt, risk assessment,
counterpart notification, clinical referral and feedback. Debriefs should distinguish avoidable administrative waiting time from time
required for testing or clinical stabilisation. A shared after-action report should record actions agreed and persons responsible, but
need not contain real patient information. Where power or mobile-network outages affect communication, an agreed backup channel
should be tested and documented.
Measurement quality is part of implementation: an independent audit should compare a sample of dashboard entries against
contemporaneous registers, document discrepancies and revise procedures without replacing the original figures invisibly. This
protects the integrity of both programme management and future peer-reviewed research.

10.3 Months seven to twelve: monitor performance fairly
A dashboard should display monthly distributions rather than only averages: median referral completion hours, interquartile ranges,
proportion of notifications acknowledged within a preregistered threshold, and complaint closure time. Results should be stratified by
crossing site and outbreak phase, with explanatory annotations for laboratory closures or exceptionally heavy movement. Aggregate
public reporting can strengthen accountability while limiting identification risk. A falling count of suspected cases should never stand
alone as evidence of progress; reduced access to screening can create the same pattern. External review should examine both
epidemiological indicators and the experience of people crossing for care or livelihood.
Measurement quality is part of implementation: an independent audit should compare a sample of dashboard entries against
contemporaneous registers, document discrepancies and revise procedures without replacing the original figures invisibly. This
protects the integrity of both programme management and future peer-reviewed research.

 10.4 Governance safeguards and escalation
The cross-border compact should distinguish clinical decisions from border-enforcement decisions. Health practitioners must be able to
recommend care without automatic punitive referral. Restrictions need a written legal basis, review date, reason-giving and an
accessible route for complaints. Data-sharing officers should maintain access logs and conduct periodic deletion reviews. An escalation
protocol must specify which agency resolves disagreement when neighbouring authorities classify the same event differently, and how
urgent patient referral continues during that disagreement. These controls do not weaken disease protection; they make cooperation
more predictable and therefore easier to sustain.
Measurement quality is part of implementation: an independent audit should compare a sample of dashboard entries against
contemporaneous registers, document discrepancies and revise procedures without replacing the original figures invisibly. This
protects the integrity of both programme management and future peer-reviewed research.

10.5 What would count as a policy success
The proposed indicators should register joint improvements in three dimensions: verified shortening of alert-to-referral time,
maintenance of access to essential care across mobility-status categories, and reduction in unjustified restrictive practices. No single
composite index should hide deterioration in equity behind gains in administrative speed. Policymakers should require a minimum
acceptable score in each domain before declaring a pilot successful. External researchers can then use phased implementation and
comparable sites to assess whether the improvements persist after initial training support is withdrawn.
Measurement quality is part of implementation: an independent audit should compare a sample of dashboard entries against
contemporaneous registers, document discrepancies and revise procedures without replacing the original figures invisibly. This
protects the integrity of both programme management and future peer-reviewed research.
